title: A state retreats; a reserve becomes vulnerable
body: Romania’s military reverses drove the government and central bank to Iași. Evacuation was a response to a real threat, not a treasure expedition. Russian pressure and guarantees enter the documentary story before shipment.
limits: A later Soviet seizure does not by itself establish a single premeditated plan stretching back through the imperial government.

title: The first deposit agreement
body: The first shipment comprised 1,738 BNR cases and two cases of Queen Marie’s jewels. The bank’s stated value was 314,580,456.84 gold lei; the jewels were separately valued at 7 million.
limits: We read published descriptions, the official table and selected original-document photographs, not the complete protocol and every annex. Do not turn the jewellery valuation into literal bullion weight.

date: Late December 1916 OS / early January 1917 NS
title: The consignment reaches Moscow
body: The first deposit was placed in the Russian State Bank’s Kremlin treasury facilities, commonly identified with the Armoury Palace. Verification continued into February.
limits: Published arrival dates differ by a day or more as well as by calendar. The site preserves a window rather than manufacturing a precise unified date.

title: An inventory becomes the reference fingerprint
body: The inventory and protocol recorded the first shipment’s contents. Later comparisons need its denominations, case numbers, weights and signatures—not merely “Romanian gold” as a label.
limits: Calendar normalization varies across retellings. BNR’s annex photograph resolves the modern table’s ten-bag discrepancy: 4,387 Austrian-crown bags, not 4,397.

title: Packing the country’s cultural memory
body: Lapedatu describes instructions, packing, George Enescu manuscripts, paintings, inspections, repeated delays and guards. On 27 July he records unloading, inspection, reloading and sealing.
limits: His charge was a subset of the cultural shipment, not all bank bullion or every institution’s property. Printed diary pp. 117–119.

title: A second agreement, not another 90 tonnes
body: The BNR component comprised 188 cases of mixed assets. Additional gold was valued at 574,523.57 gold lei—about 167 kg at the historical parity, commonly rounded to 170 kg. Much larger aggregate values included paper assets and institutional property.
limits: The frequently quoted billions of lei for the second train are not billions of lei of physical gold.

title: Lapedatu’s train actually departs
body: The diary records departure from Iași at 2 p.m., crossing the Prut later that day. The next entries place the party at Chișinău and Bender, then farther north and east.
limits: Signing on 27 July and departure on 28 July are distinct events. Published summaries sometimes collapse them. Printed pp. 118–119.

title: Follow the observed railway stops
body: Entries name Chișinău, Bender, Cherkasy, Pryluky, Bryansk and Moscow. Moscow arrival is recorded on 3 August around 10 p.m., followed by a guarded overnight stop.
limits: A projected route mentioned earlier in the diary is not identical to the observed route. Map lines connect observations, not verified railway track geometry. Printed pp. 119–120.

title: Two kinds of treasure, different rooms
body: The additional BNR gold was recorded as deposited with the earlier reserve at the Kremlin. Cultural consignments had their own storage arrangements and later moves.
limits: Do not apply every cultural-storage episode to the bank’s reserve.

title: A damp room, then a documented relocation
body: Lapedatu found ministry crates in a cramped, damp room beneath guard stairs and sought relocation. Later entries describe trucks, rain, the move to the Ssudnaia Kazna and checks on paintings. He counted 142 cases below, 38 on the ground floor and three above within his charge.
limits: Those 183 cases are not the national shipment total. The diary reports an inspected painting crate dry; damp premises are not proof that all contents were destroyed. Printed pp. 121, 129–130.

title: Plans to send treasure to America
body: The diary records anxiety about protection, a consular report after fighting, and proposals to move Academy cases via an American train. By late November the cases were to remain in Moscow.
limits: Proposed evacuation is not completed shipment. No recovered American receipt was found. Printed pp. 142, 151, 155–158.

title: Boyle brings back records and currency
body: Joseph Boyle’s mission brought archives and paper currency out of revolutionary Russia. A major scholarly biography explicitly rejects the bullion-and-crown-jewels embellishment; another article repeats a jewel story through Hill’s memoir.
limits: No inspected gold manifest proves that Boyle recovered the BNR reserve. Jewel claims require separate object-level reconciliation.

title: Seizure becomes policy
body: The Soviet authorities broke relations and declared the Romanian gold inaccessible to the Romanian oligarchy, while promising to preserve it for the Romanian people. US diplomatic reports in the following days independently document the rupture and gold dispute.
limits: This is evidence of deliberate retention, not of an unrecorded disappearance at the moment of revolution.

title: Paper currency removed
body: Moisuc, citing Schipor documents 60 and 63, describes sixteen cases of Romanian banknotes taken by Commissioner Fritsche.
limits: Banknotes are not gold. Using this episode to prove bullion financed revolutionary operations would change the asset category. Moisuc p. 72.

title: A separate lead for the royal diamonds
body: The translated retrospective report says Ganetsky took royal-family brilliants and some banknotes from the Kremlin deposit.
limits: This account conflicts with simple versions of the Boyle-jewels rescue. Original report, jewellery lists and receiving records are still required.

title: Gold is reportedly divided by currency
body: The 1924 report describes British pounds, Turkish lira and German marks sent toward “Samara–Tashkent”; Austrian crowns in 548 cases and German marks in 77 cases sent to Perm; French francs, Romanian money and other currencies left in Moscow.
limits: This is a later report reproduced through translation. “Samara–Tashkent” is an ambiguous destination or route label, not proof of a specific surviving Tashkent vault.

title: A Copenhagen rumor enters the Romanian press
body: A modern transcription of Glasul Bucovinei no. 465 reports gold—allegedly mainly Romanian 20-lei coins—pledged in Danish banks, citing an unnamed Copenhagen paper.
limits: Original issue, Danish source and bank ledgers not inspected. Coin type alone cannot establish the Moscow deposit as origin.

title: The accounting trail deserves attention
body: Pokivaylova discusses Lenin’s request to Alsky to count the gold fund, and a report due by 1 October. Schipor’s later article describes a 1 October memorandum recording Romanian gold.
limits: The full original accounts have not been read here. Pokivaylova’s 2021 statement that an Alsky report was classified is not a verified present-day access ruling.

title: A documented international gold pathway
body: US Treasury and State correspondence explains how gold with Swedish mint stamps was treated differently from visibly Soviet-origin gold. This gives a concrete records trail to examine.
limits: Generic Soviet-gold handling, not an identified Romanian shipment. The mint book and matched export/assay entries are missing.

title: The crucial proposed inventory match
body: Schipor says an RGAE report matches the 1917 deposit by denomination and proves the reserve intact at this date. If sustained by the original annexes, this sharply weakens earlier total-loss stories.
limits: We have read his account, not independently performed the complete comparison. Bookkeeping continuity must also be distinguished from a physical recount.

title: Reported return of evacuated gold to Moscow
body: Schipor’s publisher summary places the return of evacuated Romanian gold to Kremlin stores in July 1921. The later report describes overseas disposal after return.
limits: Obtain movement vouchers and receiving receipts to check which portions returned and when.

title: A real ship—and a crucial non-identification
body: The New York Assay Office rejected 7,500 imperial gold roubles tendered by J. P. Morgan & Co., consigned from the Bank of England on the Carmania.
limits: The record says Russian gold, not Romanian-deposit gold. Its proximity to the next memorandum is not proof they concern the same consignment.

title: Romania formally alleges US-bound disposal
status: Contemporary allegation in a primary record
body: The Romanian Legation told the State Department that some gold arriving in the United States came from the 1916 Moscow deposit and was being used for Soviet payments abroad.
limits: The memorandum supplies no shipment identifiers. It also precedes the autumn-1921 start in Schipor’s summary: an unresolved timing tension, not a reason to rewrite either source.

title: Gold still appears in the accounts
body: Pokivaylova cites Romanian gold in Soviet holdings at the start of 1922, but gives different balances from Osokina and Sirotkin. She points to Sokolnikov’s February reports to Lenin.
limits: The two values—105,102,337.88 and 87,074,501.05 gold roubles—must not be averaged into a fictional inventory. Scope, date and asset definitions need checking.

title: Cultural deposits are opened and inventoried
body: Published Russian and Romanian research describes commissions, movements of cases and museum/archive inventories. These create a separate, potentially item-identifiable trail.
limits: Commission totals and packing cases are not interchangeable with the original 1917 cases. Underlying lists remain a priority.

title: The best route clue points into finance
body: The translated report says French francs, British pounds and German marks were sent almost entirely abroad in installments under Narkomfin; Austrian crowns went to the State Bank’s Issue Section.
limits: No foreign recipient list is supplied in the passage. The Russian original and annexes are necessary before assigning particular banks or countries.

title: Loss of separate identity, not necessarily disappearance of metal
body: Pokivaylova describes the gold as обезличено by 1924; Schipor places final depletion by early 1925. Together they favor absorption or dispersal over an intact hidden reserve.
limits: The authors differ in explanations and numerical claims. “Depersonalized” can concern accounting identity; complete physical melting is not established by that word.

title: An accounting change is not a recovery
body: A BNR-hosted monetary history says the Moscow deposit was removed from the bank’s note-cover stock in the 1929 monetary reform.
limits: This concerns the assets qualifying as currency cover. It is not a receipt showing the gold came back, nor by itself a legal discharge of the deposit claim.

title: First major return: inspect what came back
body: The handover protocol listed 1,443 cases/bales and 27 folders/packages. Cargo traveled Moscow → Odesa → S.S. Principesa Maria → Constanța → Bucharest. BNR received 212 cases of notes, printing supplies, securities and records.
limits: These were not 1,443 gold cases. No BNR reserve was returned. Original deposit seals and a one-to-one crate identity cannot be assumed.

title: Art and historical objects return
body: A protocol was signed on 6 August; two trains reached Bucharest on 14 and 15 August. The often-cited total is 39,320 objects, including Pietroasele, paintings, coins and medals. An exhibition opened on 22 August.
limits: 33,068 coins does not mean 33,068 gold coins. Reported gold within returned objects exceeded 33 kg, not 91.5 tonnes of reserve. Published category totals differ by two objects.

title: A communist Romania asks again
body: Romania raised the bank reserve with Soviet leaders. Published accounts describe Soviet resistance and attempts to join the question to broader financial offsets.
limits: Diplomatic positions neither establish a present location nor independently settle the legal validity of offsets.

title: Twelve coins offer a bounded provenance test
body: Reports describe twelve French/Belgian coins totaling 77.09 g donated to MNIR, linked to a private return scheme.
limits: The accession and donation files have not been obtained. The coins’ age, authenticity and Moscow-deposit provenance are different questions.

title: A commission, not a recovered consignment
body: The 2003 treaty framework led to a joint historical commission, first meeting in 2004. The 2024 resolution records five meetings, the last in 2019, and a 2016 acknowledgement of authentic deposit documents.
limits: Recognition of documents and unsuccessful talks should not be reported as a return agreement.

title: Europe asks for restitution
body: The European Parliament adopted its resolution calling for return of the Romanian treasure and identifying 91.5 tonnes of fine gold.
limits: Nonbinding political resolution; not a locating operation or enforceable judgment in itself.

title: New documentation and proposed strategy
body: BNR launched a document portal in October 2025. Radio România reported a proposed recovery strategy in April 2026.
limits: No authenticated recovery or current physical holding was identified in the sources inspected for this case file. This is a research finding, not proof that no undisclosed material exists.
